    Reference · read-only, public, no login

    The Public Archive

    Every session the board has run, published as static pages anyone can read — the books ranked, all sixteen seats' grades, the Skeptic's cross-examinations, the corrections. No account and no login. The desk operator's own positions never appear, kept out by an allowlist, a sentence-level pass and a scanner that fails the build rather than publish them.

    The archive at bablytics.com/explore is the boardroom made public: one page per session, the whole book ranked, every seat's grade and note, the Skeptic's cross-examination, and the corrections the desk owed itself — exactly as written on the day.

    It is static HTML with no account and no login. That is a deliberate choice over the alternative. The app's authentication was written for one person on localhost: it hashes properly with pbkdf2, but it has no rate limiting and no abuse handling, and a shared “test account” on a findable site is a public password with extra steps. A read-only site has nothing to log into and therefore nothing to break into, and a visitor gets a URL rather than a credential.

    It is inherently in step with everything else. The archive is generated from runs/ — the same folder every briefing, court, close-out book and spotlight already pushes itself into after it is produced. The Claude artifact of a day's briefing is built from that same source. Nothing has to be kept in sync by hand, because there is only one source.

    What is not there, and how that is enforced#

    The runs archive is a mix of two things: what the board produced, which is the point of publishing, and what the desk operator holds, which is nobody else's business. Three layers separate them, and each exists because the previous one was shown to be insufficient.

    An allowlist, never a denylist
    Each document type declares the fields that may be published; everything else is dropped, including fields that do not exist yet. A denylist fails open — a field added next round would publish itself by default and nobody would notice until it was indexed. It also mangles the writing: this board produces prose like “Azure past $100B banked” and “not how an owner acquires a business”, and a keyword filter butchers both.
    A sentence-level pass inside allowed text
    The allowlist protects fields, not the inside of them. Board prose occasionally mentions the operator's own book mid-paragraph. Any single sentence carrying a high-precision marker is dropped and replaced with a note that a line was removed; every other sentence is left untouched. Across the whole archive this has fired once.
    A scanner that fails the build
    Before any page is written, the rendered output is scanned for the operator's actual figures. A hit raises and nothing is published. The gate runs again inside publish.sh, so a stale build cannot reach a public repository.
    Two holes the gate found in itself, which is the argument for having one. The first build was refused: a briefing's prose said “RTX and IWM remain OPEN” inside an allowlisted field — the case a field-level allowlist cannot catch, and the reason the sentence pass exists. Then a subtler one: html.escape turns every apostrophe into &#x27;, so owner's record became owner&#x27;s record and no pattern containing an apostrophe could match a rendered page. The gate had been passing pages it should have stopped; the one leak it did catch only tripped because that phrase happened to have no apostrophe in it. The scanner now reads both the raw and the unescaped form, and its self-test asserts it catches the escaped version of every marker.

    Verifying it rather than asserting it#

    The redaction module carries a self_test that the build runs before it writes anything. It asserts the scanner catches four known operator markers and their HTML-escaped forms, that it does not fire on four real sentences of board prose, and that the sentence scrubber removes the offending sentence while keeping the ones around it. A scanner nobody proved is a comfort, not a control.

    What a visitor sees#

    • An index of every session, newest first, with the headline the board actually wrote.
    • Per session: the executive summary, the standing read, how the document was produced, the correction the desk owed, the whole book ranked with entries, stops, targets and written kills, the room's range and the Skeptic's grade per lead, the house rules, the branches and the checks.
    • The Fund's and the Spotlight's verdicts for that day — including the days on which the correct answer was that nothing cleared sixty.
    Research output, and it says so on every page. Grades, levels and structures are model output rather than recommendations, none of it is financial advice, and nothing in Bablytics places, stages or routes an order of any kind.
